title: Small Kakeya sets in F_3^6 and F_3^7
made_with: AI agents working in MV2's name (MV2, Munim, Inc.); not checked by a human mathematician
definition: K in F_3^n is a Kakeya set if for every nonzero direction d it contains a full line {a, a+d, a+2d}; k_n is the least size of a Kakeya set in F_3^n

7.structure: the layer x0 = 0 is exactly the 105-point set of F_3^6; layers x0 = 1 and 2 add 56 + 50 = 106 points, which is 2 * 53

earlier.note: first set below the pattern value 107; superseded by the 105-point set the same day
first set below the classical 255, equal to the pattern value 213; superseded by the 211-point set the same day

3.source: V. F. Lev, computer search, 2009 (blog comment)

4.source: upper bound Lev 2009; lower bound by our computer proof PROOF26.md, not human-checked

5.source: upper bound Chung, Du and Wesley arXiv:2608.23691; lower bound our k5/QUAD45.md and k5/SD2.md, not human-checked

asymptotic_constructions: Kopparty, Lev, Saraf and Sudan (arXiv:1003.3736, Theorem 8) give Kakeya sets in F_3^n of size (3 / 2^(2/3))^(n + O(sqrt n)), base about 1.8899, by a random construction; it gives no explicit sets for small n

lev_pattern.source: V. F. Lev, comment 994 on T. Tao's blog, 14 March 2009: 'I am very curious to know whether k_5 = 53: notice the pattern in 3, 7, 13, 27, 53, ...'; Chung, Du and Wesley (arXiv:2608.23691) state it as the recurrence k_n = k_(n-1) + 2 k_(n-2) and say whether it continues remains open
lev_pattern.consequence: k_6 <= 105 < 107 and k_7 <= 211 < 213. Since k_2 = 7 and k_3 = 13, the recurrence cannot hold at all of n = 4, 5, 6: if it did, k_6 would be 107. With k_4 = 27 it fails at n = 5 or n = 6: either k_5 <= 52, or k_5 = 53 and k_6 <= 105 = k_5 + 2 k_4 - 2.

recurrence_on_true_values.note: if k_7 <= k_6 + 2 k_5 held, k_7 would be at most 105 + 2 * 53 = 211; the 211-point set reaches exactly this value, as a 105-point layer plus 106 = 2 * 53 points in the other two layers

layer_observation.note: In every dimension we tried, a search that keeps a record Kakeya set A of F_3^(n-1) fixed in one layer needed about 2 k_(n-2) more points in the other two layers: 53 + 54 = 107 in F_3^6 (round 1, best of one run), 105 + 106 = 211 and 106 + 107 = 213 in F_3^7 (round 3). This is an observation from stalled searches, not a theorem; k8/layer.py tests it directly.

search_log.note: first_reached lists (size, seconds) when each size was first reached; intermediate entries omitted. Every final set was re-checked by k5.walk.is_kakeya in the run, and the record sets are re-checked by k6/test_sets.py (and the 211-point set also by k6/test_layers.py) at every commit. 'structure' numbers were printed by k6/probe2.py stats(): lines = number of full lines in the set, single_line_directions = directions covered by exactly one line, removable_points = points whose removal keeps the set Kakeya, section_min/max = smallest and largest of the 3 x 364 (or 3 x 1093) hyperplane sections, K_cap_minus_K = |K intersect -K|.
